example: I firmly believe that every student should learn to cook.
From my perspective, small classes work better.
note: Not 'in my perspective'.

example: I am convinced that reading daily improves writing.

meaning: a softer way to give an opinion
example: It seems to me that the rule is outdated.

meaning: introduces a position you will defend
example: I would argue that homework still has value.

term: as far as I am concerned
example: As far as I'm concerned, the benefits outweigh the costs.
note: About your opinion, not your knowledge. For knowledge use 'as far as I know'.

meaning: I usually think; a modest opinion
example: I tend to think that people learn best by doing.
In my view, the city needs more parks.
note: Do not write 'in my point of view'. Say 'from my point of view'.

example: I am inclined to believe that the second option is safer.

term: there is no doubt in my mind that
example: There is no doubt in my mind that she deserved the prize.
Personally speaking, I'd rather walk than drive.

term: I would go so far as to say
example: I would go so far as to say it changed my life.
The plan is popular; however, it is expensive.
note: Between two sentences use a period or semicolon before it, never just a comma.

meaning: compares two different facts in one sentence
example: My brother loves crowds, whereas I prefer quiet places.

meaning: introduces the other side of an issue
example: City life is exciting. On the other hand, it can be exhausting.
The north is dry. In contrast, the south gets heavy rain.
More practice builds confidence; conversely, avoiding practice increases fear.
note: Too formal for speaking tasks.

example: The exam was hard. Nevertheless, most students passed.
It was raining; nonetheless, the match continued.

meaning: when compared with the previous thing
example: My old school was huge. By comparison, this one feels like a family.
The test wasn't easy. On the contrary, it was the hardest this year.
note: Only to deny the previous statement. It does NOT mean 'on the other hand'.

example: While some students enjoy group work, others find it stressful.

meaning: but, with a sense of surprise
example: The instructions were simple, yet many people misread them.
The course is demanding. That said, I'd recommend it.
Admittedly, the project took longer than planned.

meaning: in spite of the fact that
example: Although it was expensive, it was worth it.
note: Never follow with 'but' in the same sentence.

example: Even though I was tired, I finished the essay.
note: Not 'even although'.

meaning: I accept that this is true
example: Granted, online classes are convenient, but they can be lonely.
Despite the rain, the festival went ahead.
note: Never 'despite of'. Followed by a noun or -ing form.

example: In spite of her nerves, she spoke clearly.
note: Three words, and it keeps the 'of'.

meaning: accepts a point before answering it
example: While it is true that cars are convenient, they pollute our cities.
The plan worked, albeit slowly.
note: Never before a full clause. Avoid in speaking.

example: It could be argued that uniforms limit self-expression.
To be fair, the teacher did warn us in advance.
He missed the bus. Consequently, he was late for the exam.
The road was closed. As a result, we took a longer route.
The evidence is weak; therefore, the claim should be rejected.
She practiced daily and thus improved quickly.
The data were incomplete; hence the delay.
note: Too formal for speaking.

example: The match was postponed owing to heavy rain.
note: Followed by a noun, not a clause.

example: The delay was due to a technical fault.
note: Followed by a noun: 'due to the rain', not 'due to it rained'.

example: Many of his problems stem from a lack of sleep.
Skipping breakfast can lead to poor concentration.
note: After 'lead to', use a noun or -ing: 'lead to improving', not 'lead to improve'.

example: The new policy gave rise to a heated debate.

meaning: to be one of the causes of
example: Regular exercise contributes to better mental health.
note: After 'contribute to', use -ing: 'contributes to reducing stress'.

example: The trip was canceled on account of the storm.

meaning: because of what was just said
example: Water is scarce here. For this reason, every drop is valued.

meaning: and that then causes the next thing
example: Reading builds vocabulary, which in turn improves writing.
Some skills, for instance cooking, are best learned at home.
To illustrate, consider how children learn their first language.

meaning: a clear example of what I mean
example: Technology can unite people. A case in point is video calling.
Outdoor activities such as hiking reduce stress.
note: Do not end the list with 'etc.' after 'such as'.

meaning: introduces the specific thing you mean
example: Two subjects, namely math and physics, were the hardest.

meaning: a spoken way to introduce an example
example: Take my school, for example — we have no library.
I enjoy science, biology in particular.
Interest is growing, as evidenced by rising enrollment.
This is exemplified by the success of community libraries.

meaning: in fact; adds force to a statement
example: The task was difficult; indeed, few finished it.
She is undoubtedly the strongest candidate.
The last chapter is particularly moving.
A good teacher is patient, clear and, above all, fair.

meaning: in a large or important way
example: Prices have risen significantly this year.

meaning: adds a stronger or surprising detail
example: I wasn't bored. In fact, I stayed an extra hour.

meaning: in a way that is extremely important
example: Crucially, the scholarship also covers housing.

meaning: draws attention to an important point
example: It is worth noting that attendance doubled in one year.
Several cities, notably Addis Ababa, are growing fast.
It was by far the best trip of my life.
The course is free. Moreover, it includes a certificate.
note: Sounds stiff in speech; say 'on top of that'.

example: The park is small. Furthermore, it closes early.
note: Avoid in speaking tasks.

example: In addition, students receive weekly feedback.
I don't want to go. Besides, it's too late.
note: 'Beside' (no s) means 'next to'.

example: It not only saves time but also reduces stress.
note: Keep both halves parallel: verb + verb, or noun + noun.

example: The food was delicious. What's more, it was cheap.

meaning: introduces a point of the same weight
example: Equally important, students need time to rest.
I was late, and on top of that I forgot my notes.
In conclusion, the advantages clearly outweigh the risks.
To sum up, practice matters more than talent.
In short, the policy helps everyone involved.
Overall, it was a valuable experience.
All things considered, I would choose the smaller college.
Ultimately, the decision belongs to the student.
On balance, the change has been positive.
Taking everything into account, I support the proposal.
It appears that they are waiting for a bus.

meaning: probably, based on what I can see
example: She is presumably the owner of the shop.
This is arguably the city's most beautiful street.
I agree to some extent, but the cost worries me.
Teenagers tend to sleep later than adults.
The price is likely to rise next year.

meaning: in a way that appears true
example: He solved the seemingly impossible puzzle in minutes.
It seems as though the market has just opened.

meaning: using this as evidence for a guess
example: Judging by their uniforms, they are students.
This might well be his first day at work.
The girl looks completely focused on her drawing.
A cheerful vendor is greeting his customers.
The runners look exhausted but proud.
She has a determined look on her face.

meaning: so interested that you notice nothing else
example: The man is engrossed in his newspaper.
note: Always 'engrossed in', not 'engrossed with'.

example: Two casually dressed students are chatting outside.
An elderly couple is walking along the beach.
note: More polite than 'old'.

example: A middle-aged woman is selling fruit.

meaning: moving the hands to express something
example: The teacher is gesturing toward the board.

meaning: resting the body against or toward something
example: A boy is leaning against the wall, waiting.

meaning: looking steadily for a long time
example: The child is gazing at the birds overhead.
The students seem enthusiastic about the experiment.
note: 'enthusiastic about', not 'enthusiastic for'.

meaning: slow to act because of doubt
example: He looks hesitant, as if he is unsure of the answer.
Everyone on the platform is absorbed in their phones.
The photo shows a bustling morning market.
The platform is crowded with commuters.
note: 'crowded with', not 'crowded of'.

example: They are sitting in a bright, spacious kitchen.

meaning: untidy, covered with too many things
example: His desk is cluttered with books and cups.
It looks like a cozy neighborhood cafe.
note: American spelling; British is 'cosy'.

example: The lake looks serene in the early light.

meaning: full of color, energy and life
example: The street is decorated in vibrant colors.
They are working in a dimly lit workshop.
This seems to be a rural area with few buildings.
It is a typical urban scene: traffic, noise and tall buildings.

meaning: in the front part of the picture
example: In the foreground, a dog is sleeping on the steps.
note: One word: foreground.

meaning: in the far part of the picture
example: In the background, I can make out some mountains.

meaning: on the left of the picture
example: On the left-hand side, there is a row of bicycles.

meaning: with a view of, from above
example: They are on a balcony overlooking the sea.
The house is surrounded by tall trees.

meaning: spread over an area without order
example: Toys are scattered across the floor.
My confidence gradually improved.
The city is growing rapidly.
Attendance has risen steadily since January.

meaning: to experience a change or process
example: The neighborhood has undergone major changes.
note: Past: underwent; participle: undergone.

meaning: a change in position or direction
example: There has been a shift toward online learning.
Interest in the club declined after the summer.
There was a surge in applications this year.

meaning: to keep going up and down
example: Prices fluctuate depending on the season.
The results demonstrate the value of regular practice.
His smile indicates that the news is good.
The story highlights the importance of honesty.
My teacher always emphasized clear handwriting.
note: No preposition: 'emphasize the point', not 'emphasize on'.

meaning: to accept that something is true
example: I acknowledge that the plan has risks.
Schools must address the issue of bullying.
Group projects enhance communication skills.
Team sports foster a sense of belonging.
Constant criticism can undermine a child's confidence.
Technology facilitates communication across borders.
The scholarship enabled her to study abroad.
note: Pattern: enable someone TO do something.

meaning: to make a determined effort to deal with
example: The city is finally tackling its traffic problem.
Tourism generates income for local families.

meaning: to make clear with an example
example: This example illustrates my point well.

meaning: to judge the quality or amount of
example: Exams assess memory more than understanding.

meaning: to keep at the same level; to claim
example: It is hard to maintain friendships across long distances.

meaning: to try to achieve over time
example: I plan to pursue a degree in engineering.
Children acquire languages remarkably fast.
Traveling broadens your understanding of the world.

meaning: to treat as more important than other things
example: I had to prioritize sleep over social media.
Regular breaks are beneficial for concentration.
note: 'beneficial for' or 'beneficial to'.

example: Too much screen time is detrimental to sleep.
note: 'detrimental to', not 'detrimental for'.

example: Sleep is crucial for memory.
note: Already extreme: not 'very crucial'.

example: Clean water is essential for health.
note: Not 'very essential'.

meaning: large or important enough to notice
example: There was a significant improvement in her grades.
The project required considerable effort.

meaning: large in size, value or importance
example: She won a substantial scholarship.
Some mistakes are inevitable when you learn.

meaning: existing in many places or among many people
example: There is widespread support for the new library.
Banning phones in schools is a controversial idea.
She gave a compelling reason for her choice.
A daily bus service is not feasible in such a small town.
Tutoring younger students was a rewarding experience.

meaning: needing a lot of effort or skill
example: Medicine is a demanding field of study.
Her advice was invaluable during my first year.
note: Means VERY valuable, not 'without value'.

meaning: having the opposite effect to the one intended
example: Studying all night before an exam is counterproductive.
The social aspect of school matters as much as the lessons.

meaning: one of the things that causes a result
example: Cost was the deciding factor.
The teacher had a lasting impact on me.
note: 'impact on', not 'impact to'.

example: The main drawback of the plan is its cost.
One clear benefit of cycling is better health.

meaning: a way of thinking about something
example: Living abroad gave me a new perspective.

meaning: a way of dealing with something
example: We need a different approach to teaching math.
note: 'approach to', followed by a noun or -ing.

example: Learning to speak in public was a real challenge.
The exchange program was a rare opportunity.
note: 'opportunity to do', not 'opportunity of doing' in most cases.

example: I have a tendency to leave things until the last minute.

meaning: a result, often a negative one
example: Every choice has consequences.
My top priority this year is improving my English.

meaning: buys a second to think, naturally
example: That's an interesting question. I'd say it depends on the person.
note: Use once per test at most, or it sounds rehearsed.

example: Let me think — probably when I was about ten.
Well, I'd have to say my grandmother.
To be honest, I've never enjoyed team sports.

meaning: in fact; adds a small surprise
example: Actually, I changed my mind about that last year.
note: Means 'in fact', NOT 'currently'.

example: What I mean is, the rule is fair but badly explained.
The way I see it, both sides have a point.

meaning: signals a memory you are not fully sure of
example: If I remember correctly, it was the summer of 2023.
The student explained that she had missed two classes.
He mentioned that the deadline had moved.
The advisor suggested that she apply early.
note: After 'suggested that', use the base verb: 'that she apply'. Never 'suggested her to'.

example: The professor recommended that he narrow the topic.
note: Base verb after 'that': 'that he narrow'. Never 'recommended him to'.

example: She pointed out that the library closes at six.

meaning: accepted a plan / shared an opinion
example: The professor agreed to extend the deadline.
note: 'agreed to' + verb for actions; 'agreed that' + clause for opinions.

example: The student asked about the scholarship requirements.
The librarian advised her to request the book early.
note: Pattern: advised someone TO do something.

example: He reminded her to bring a note from the clinic.

meaning: said they were willing to do something
example: Her classmate offered to share his notes.
